items.title: Ioannidis argued most published research findings are false
items.claim: John Ioannidis's 2005 PLoS Medicine paper made what claim?

options.text: Most published research findings are false — because of low prior probability of true effects, low power, flexibility in analysis, and selective reporting; the title was 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False'

items.reveal:
Ioannidis used a Bayesian framework: a positive finding's probability of being true depends on prior probability of the hypothesis, power, type I error rate and bias. For exploratory research with many tested hypotheses and small studies, the probability that a 'significant' result is true can be below 50%.

The Open Science Collaboration's 2015 Science paper directly tested this in psychology: of 100 replications, 36% were significant in the same direction as the original. Effect sizes averaged about half the original. Hardly any of those original findings were obviously wrong; many were inflated by methodological flexibility.
items.why: The replication crisis isn't unique to psychology — it has hit medicine, economics, marketing and machine learning. The methodological response (preregistration, larger samples, registered reports) is reshaping research practice.

items.title: The magical number seven
items.claim: George Miller's 1956 paper proposed a famous limit on short-term memory. What was the span?
items.reveal:
Miller's 1956 paper 'The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two' described short-term memory span as roughly 5 to 9 items.

Later work by Cowan (2001) revised the effective limit to around 4 chunks once rehearsal is controlled.
items.why: Capacity depends on how information is grouped. Chunking effectively expands what fits in working memory.

items.title: Flow requires challenge matching skill
items.claim: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's flow research (1975 onwards) identified conditions for the optimal experience. What characterises flow?

options.text: Challenge matched to skill (slightly stretching), clear goals, immediate feedback, deep concentration, sense of control, loss of self-consciousness, time distortion

items.reveal:
Csikszentmihalyi's Experience Sampling Method (ESM, 1975) gave participants pagers; when paged at random they noted what they were doing and how they felt. The pattern: deep enjoyment occurred when skill and challenge were both high.

Too little challenge → boredom; too much → anxiety. Sports psychology uses flow frameworks for performance preparation. Critics (Engeser 2012) note flow may be more available in certain activity types and that measurement post-hoc is suspect.
items.why: Flow describes a measurable state but doesn't make it easy to engineer. The conditions can be designed for; the experience can't be commanded.
